title: What Happens When You Get a Paper Cut?
description:
Send this to the friend who acts like a paper cut is a war wound.
A paper cut usually heals in two to three days, but your fingertips are packed with nerve endings, so one tiny slice hits far more of them than the same cut on your back. Tiny blood vessels under the skin of your fingers make it bleed more, and the sting is protective: it makes you baby the cut so it heals (Ohio State Wexner Medical Center). If a cut isn't getting better, especially if you have diabetes or a weak immune system, Ohio State says see a doctor to check for infection.

structure_note: Three beats, no diary, no lineup, no showdown. Beat 1 (nerve map): from the frame-1 fingertip on the paper edge, zoom into an x-ray fingertip that lights up like a dense city map of cyan nerve lines; split screen with a sparse back map, one identical slice crossing both (many lit nerves vs a few); on 'less about the size, more about the spot' a ruler shows both slices are the same length while a pin drops on the fingertip. Re-hook: hard zoom under the fingertip skin into a mesh of tiny red capillaries (new scene, schematic, no gore: three neat dots of red only). Relatable beat: the hero staring at a barely visible cut with a comically big bandage. Reveal: a shield labelled GUARD snaps over the finger, pill B gets the check, the hero holds the finger carefully away from the keyboard. Safety line: a calm clinic-door icon. Tease, then cut back to the frame-1 fingertip on the paper edge.
safety: Curious-friend tone, no personal medical advice beyond Ohio State's 'if it doesn't improve, especially with diabetes, see a doctor' guidance. No gore: blood is three small schematic dots, the cut is a thin line, never an open wound. All claims from one medical source (Ohio State Wexner); popular non-medical claims (paper 'saws' skin, no clot, chemicals in paper) were left out because no medical source backs them.
